title: Polymer clay faux malachite pendant
subtitle: Banded concentric ring pattern in green polymer clay imitating malachite
excerpt: Malachite's distinctive concentric banded pattern is recreated in polymer clay using alternating logs of light and dark green, rolled and sliced to reveal the circular cross-section. No kiln is required: the pendant hardens in a domestic oven at 130°C.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Faux-stone polymer clay methods are a widely documented craft technique; no specific copyright source reproduced.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling material that hardens in a domestic oven at 110 to 130°C; not a true ceramic
A cylinder of polymer clay with a pattern running through its full length; sliced to reveal the same cross-section image on every slice

content.text: Malachite has a banded ring pattern that appears when the mineral is cut cross-section. The same effect in
polymer clay
comes from building concentrically layered
canes

of alternating light and dark green, then cutting slices from them to cover a pendant base. No kiln is required: the piece hardens in a standard domestic oven. The finished pendant is a hard decorative plastic, not a ceramic, and should not come into contact with food.

materials.name: Polymer clay, light green or jade
Jump ring and pendant bail (metal, for hanging)
Fine sandpaper (400 and 800 grit) for finishing

tools.name: Pottery rolling pin or acrylic roller

content.text: Conditioning the clay

Warm each colour in your hands and roll it repeatedly until it is smooth, pliable, and free of cracks at the fold. Unconditioned polymer clay crumbles when sliced. Condition each colour separately to avoid mixing them at this stage.
Building the malachite cane
Roll the white clay into a thin log about 4 mm in diameter and 5 cm long. This is the innermost ring of the cane.

Roll the light green clay into a thin sheet about 2 mm thick. Wrap it around the white log to form a 2 mm thick layer. Trim the overlap cleanly and roll the wrapped log gently on the work surface to smooth the join.
Wrap a 2 mm layer of dark green around the light green layer. Roll to smooth.
Repeat the wrapping sequence once more: a 1 mm layer of light green, then a 1 mm layer of dark green. The finished cane should be about 12 mm in diameter.

Make 3 to 5 smaller canes using the same process but starting with a 2 mm white log, building out to about 6 mm in diameter. These smaller canes create the natural variation of real malachite, where ring clusters of different sizes sit alongside each other.

Group the large cane and small canes together in a bundle. Press the gaps between them with thin rolls of dark green clay to fill the spaces. Roll the bundle gently to compact it into a solid cylinder about 20 mm in diameter.
Cutting and forming the pendant
Slice the cane cleanly with a sharp blade, cutting slices about 2 mm thick. The cross-section of each slice reveals the concentric ring pattern.
Roll a small slab of dark green clay about 5 mm thick. Cut a rectangle or oval roughly 3 cm by 2 cm from it. This is the pendant base.

Press slices from the cane side by side onto the pendant base, covering the entire surface. Roll gently with a smooth roller to press the slices flat and level with each other. The cane patterns will distort slightly as they press together, creating the organic swirled look of natural stone.
Pierce a small hole at the top of the pendant with a needle tool for the bail or jump ring. Press the hole through cleanly so it does not collapse during curing.
Curing

Place the pendant on a ceramic tile or piece of card (not directly on a baking tray as the tray surface may flatten the underside). Cure in a domestic oven at 130°C for 30 minutes. Use a dedicated oven thermometer to verify temperature: most domestic ovens run 10 to 20°C above their dial setting. Do not share the curing oven with food cookware. Ventilate the kitchen during curing.
Finishing

Once cool, sand through 400 then 800 grit sandpaper under water to remove the matte surface and reveal a stone-like sheen. Buff with a soft cloth or a polishing pad for a deeper gloss. Thread a jump ring through the hole and attach a bail.
Use and care
Cured polymer clay is a hard decorative plastic. Not food-safe. Not suitable for the dishwasher or microwave. Keep away from strong solvents. Wipe clean with a damp cloth.
Variations
Use blue and white to create a faux azurite or lapis lazuli effect. Use orange and terracotta tones for a faux carnelian look.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Slices crack when cut from the cane
items.cause: The clay was too cold and stiff, or was not conditioned enough before building
items.fix: Warm the cane briefly in cupped hands for 2 minutes before slicing. Use a very sharp blade and cut with a single clean downward press rather than a sawing motion

items.problem: The malachite rings blur into one colour when pressed flat
items.cause: Too much rolling pressure spread the colours together
items.fix: Use only light rolling pressure to level the slices. The slight ridges from individual slices smooth out during curing without overworking the pattern

items.problem: Pendant surface shows fingerprint marks after curing
items.cause: The clay surface was touched after final shaping
items.fix: Sand the surface lightly with 400-grit sandpaper once cured. Buff dry with a soft cloth
